EDCOR 310 · Reading Menu

Joy of Learning

Joy of Learning readings are where you get to follow a question, meet a compelling idea, or explore a debate beyond the course textbook.

How this works

The requirement. Each week, spend about one hour with readings from the current unit's menu: articles, talks, podcasts, videos, essays, and more.

Choose your path. Pick the readings that genuinely interest you. The times are rough stopping points, not always the full runtime. When a reading says “~20 min,” spend about 20 minutes with it and then move on. If you want to keep going, see extra credit below.

Use the jigsaw. Divide the options among your group so each person studies something different, then teach your reading back to the group. The goal is to keep overlap low and get the most learning for the whole group.

Learn actively. As you read or listen, find the author's main claim, the evidence or reasoning behind it, and one point that surprised, challenged, or interested you. Be ready to explain the material in your own words.

Make it useful. In your prep checks, explain what you read and show your notes. If you read extra for extra credit, provide slides that cover all of your sources (not just the first hour) and a short video recording explaining what you read and what you learned. Name your favorite ideas, explain how they will change you, and connect the material to educational psychology, teaching, human development, or your own life.

Keep an open mind. Some readings are compelling, intriguing, controversial, or even divisive. You do not have to agree with everything you read. Your job is to understand the argument fairly, evaluate it thoughtfully, and add something worthwhile to the conversation.

Extra credit. One hour is required. Each extra hour of real engagement earns extra credit worth half as much as the hour before: 2 hours → 15/10, 3 hours → 17.5/10, and so on, up to a maximum of 20/10.

AI and the other readings. Joy of Learning readings are separate from the Applied Readings and the course textbook. You may use AI to clarify a difficult idea after you have engaged with the material yourself, but your group should hear your understanding of the reading, not an AI-generated substitute for it.

Using this page. Press “I’ll read this” to track your minutes against the unit’s requirement, and “My group has it” for readings a groupmate has claimed. Your picks are saved in this browser only. “Copy my list” gives you your readings and links to paste wherever you need them.

Unit 1

Introduction to Psychology

Weeks 1–4 · Chapters 1–8

Where educational psychology begins: what education is for, why human judgment needs help, how evidence improves professional practice, why science has limits, and what it might mean to build a life and classroom that flourish.

Week 1

3 readings · 1 hr 50 min of options
ReadingFormat / lensTimePlanBang for buck
Coddling vs. Strengthening University (opens in a new tab) WatchPurpose / challenge ~30 min +

Should education protect students from difficulty? Jonathan Haidt argues that students become stronger when education exposes them to challenge, disagreement, and the possibility of being wrong. A lively opening argument about what college is supposed to do and what kind of person learning should form.

YouTube — watch about 30 minutes.

Rethinking Fast and Slow: The Importance of Intuition (opens in a new tab) ReadJudgment / intuition ~20 min +

Is intuition always the enemy of good thinking? Carl Hendrick revisits the relationship between fast and slow thinking and asks when intuition reflects expertise rather than bias. A useful counterweight to the simple story that careful reasoning is good and intuition is bad.

Carl Hendrick on Substack — read for up to 20 minutes.

What Really Works in Teaching and Learning (opens in a new tab) ListenTeaching / evidence-informed practice ~60 min +

What does effective teaching actually look like? Carl Hendrick surveys the research behind explicit instruction, teacher talk, motivation, assessment, professional development, and the role of AI in education. A wide-ranging, practical conversation about turning research into better classroom practice, and about telling genuinely useful ideas from fashionable ones.

The EduDisruptor Podcast with Carl Hendrick — listen for up to 60 minutes.

Week 2

7 readings · 3 hr 45 min of options
ReadingFormat / lensTimePlanBang for buck
The Holy Art of Skepticism (lecture) (opens in a new tab) WatchEvidence / epistemology ~60 min +

Skepticism is not cynicism. In his William James Lecture in Psychology, Benjamin Pacini (your instructor) treats skepticism as an intellectual virtue: a disciplined willingness to ask what we know, how we know it, and what would change our minds. This is the big, slow-thinking option.

William James Lecture in Psychology (2024) — watch about 60 minutes.

Pairs with: The Holy Art of Skepticism (essay series)

The Holy Art of Skepticism (essay series) (opens in a new tab) ReadEvidence / epistemology ~60 min +

Rather read than watch? The written version of the same argument, in a series of essays by Benjamin Pacini. Start with Part I and keep going through the series. Choose this or the lecture, not both.

Benjamin Pacini on Substack — read until you reach about 60 minutes.

Pairs with: The Holy Art of Skepticism (lecture)

The Oedipus Trap (opens in a new tab) ListenEvidence / professional practice ~30 min +

What happens when a theory becomes impossible to escape? A case study in how compelling stories can become self-confirming explanations. The Oedipus story gives you a memorable way to think about bias, professional judgment, and the danger of interpreting every outcome as proof that the theory was right.

EconTalk with Megan McArdle — listen for about 30 minutes.

Why Do School Psychs Cling to Ineffective Practices? (opens in a new tab) ListenEvidence / institutions ~15 min +

Why do trained professionals hold on to weak ideas? This short piece asks why evidence does not automatically dislodge familiar practices. It is a direct invitation to think about professional responsibility, institutional incentives, and what it means to practice education well.

School Psyched Podcast (about 68 minutes) — listen for 15 minutes.

Visible Learning, Part 1: Disasters and Below-Average Methods (opens in a new tab) WatchEvidence / impact ~15 min +

What does it mean to say that something works? John Hattie walks through teaching methods whose average effects are weak, or worse. Listen for how he compares effects across studies, and ask whether a small difference would matter in a real classroom.

John Hattie talk — watch the whole thing. Watch Part 1 before Part 2.

Pairs with: Visible Learning, Part 2: Effective Methods

Visible Learning, Part 2: Effective Methods (opens in a new tab) WatchEvidence / impact ~15 min +

Which methods clear the bar, and how high is the bar? The second half of Hattie's talk turns to methods with stronger average effects. Pay attention to the yardstick he uses to call something effective, and to what an effect size can and can't tell a teacher.

John Hattie talk — watch the whole thing.

Pairs with: Visible Learning, Part 1: Disasters and Below-Average Methods

Sold a Story: The Problem (opens in a new tab) ListenResearch to practice ~30 min +

How does an educational idea become common before it is well tested? This episode follows the consequences of a widely adopted approach to reading instruction. It is a compelling case study of the research-to-practice gap and of how good intentions, institutional momentum, and persuasive stories can outrun evidence.

American Public Media — listen to Episode 1 for about 30 minutes.

Week 3

7 readings · 2 hr 35 min of options
ReadingFormat / lensTimePlanBang for buck
The Replication Crisis (opens in a new tab) ListenScience / uncertainty ~30 min +

What should we do when science gets something wrong? A story about failed replications, scientific self-correction, and the uncomfortable distance between a published finding and a dependable truth. The goal is not to lose faith in science, but to understand why good science needs humility, repetition, and revision.

You Are Not So Smart — listen for about 30 minutes.

The Rise and Fall of Peer Review (opens in a new tab) ReadScience / institutions ~30 min +

Who watches the watchers of science? Adam Mastroianni examines peer review as a necessary but imperfect institution. This is a chance to think about how knowledge is filtered, how quality control can fail, and why the imperfections of science do not make every claim equally credible.

Adam Mastroianni — read for about 30 minutes.

Social Psychology Won't Save Us (opens in a new tab) ListenScience / limits ~30 min +

Can a scientific explanation solve a human problem by itself? This conversation pushes against overconfident applications of social psychology. It asks you to distinguish a useful scientific finding from the temptation to treat one study, one effect, or one framework as a complete answer to a human question.

Art of Manliness — listen for about 30 minutes.

#fakescience (opens in a new tab) ListenScience / public claims ~30 min +

Why does bad science spread so easily? A public-facing story about scientific fraud, hype, incentives, and the conditions that reward confident claims. It offers a concrete way to explore why the scientific method matters and why institutions still need wise judgment.

The Weeds — listen for about 30 minutes.

The Scandal That Shook Psychology to Its Core (opens in a new tab) WatchResearch / replication ~10 min +

What happens when a field's most famous findings fail to replicate? This short video introduces a scandal in psychology and the larger questions it raises about replication, publication incentives, statistical practices, and scientific self-correction. Use it to distinguish a flawed study from a flawed scientific enterprise.

Neuro Transmissions (the video runs about 30 minutes) — stop around 10.

Also available: BYU-Idaho copy

Is Most Published Research Wrong? (opens in a new tab) WatchResearch / evidence ~10 min +

Is the published literature more certain than the evidence beneath it? This short video asks why published research can look more definitive than the underlying evidence. Bring back one way that publication practices, incentives, or selective reporting can shape what gets noticed.

Veritasium — watch the whole thing.

Also available: BYU-Idaho copy

Are Most Papers Never Cited? (opens in a new tab) ReadResearch / institutions ~15 min +

What does it mean if much of the research we publish is rarely used? This short article examines how often academic papers are cited, read, or forgotten. Ask whether citation counts measure importance, visibility, usefulness, or merely attention, and what that means for how we evaluate knowledge.

LSE Impact Blog — read the whole article.

Is flourishing more than feeling good? A quick explainer on what positive psychology studies and why it doesn't reduce happiness to a single feeling. A good warm-up for Seligman's talk.

TED talk — watch the whole thing.

Unit 2

Developmental Psychology

Weeks 5–7 · Chapters 9–14

What shapes a person? Unit 2 moves from the early environment of parenting and play through sex, gender, adolescence, morality, mindset, personality, and agency. These readings ask not only what develops, but how much our choices and circumstances can change us.

Unit 3

Motivational Psychology

Weeks 8–10 · Chapters 15–20

By what are we motivated? Unit 3 is about what moves us: personality, culture, community, and finally, agency. These readings ask whether we choose to move or whether our biology moves us. They also build a foundation for a future teacher's work in managing classroom behavior and sculpting souls: character development and effective classroom culture.

How One Tweet Can Ruin Your Life (opens in a new tab) WatchShame / social life ~20 min +

Jon Ronson at TED — watch the whole thing.

Durkheim on Suicide (opens in a new tab) WatchSociology / belonging ~10 min +

What if a deeply personal act is partly shaped by the strength of a person's social bonds? Durkheim's classic argument treats social integration and regulation as central to understanding suicide. Focus on the sociological idea rather than trying to master every detail, and be ready to explain what an individual-level account might miss.

The School of Life — watch the whole thing.

The Great Behaviorism Manifesto (opens in a new tab) ReadBehaviorism / learning ~30 min +

What if behaviorism is more powerful, more humane, and more misunderstood than people think? Benjamin Pacini makes the strongest case he can for behaviorism as a practical science of changing environments and behavior. You do not need to agree with the manifesto; you do need to identify its best argument and the point at which you resist it.

Benjamin Pacini on Substack — read for about 30 minutes.

In Praise of Shame (opens in a new tab) ReadShame / moral formation ~30 min +

Can shame ever be a force for good? This essay offers a deliberately provocative argument about shame, conscience, and moral formation. Read it as an argument to test: distinguish useful moral discomfort from humiliation, and ask what kind of shame helps a person return rather than retreat.

Benjamin Pacini on Substack — read Part I.

Unit 4

Cognitive Psychology

Weeks 11–13 · Chapters 21–26

How does the brain learn? Unit 4 is true educational psychology: memory, learning, attention, and how to change minds that want to stay stubborn. These readings are essential for anyone engaged in the business of soulcraft, beginning with how to capture attention and ending with protecting yourself from the pressures of the school you will end up in.
